newsitem.title: USA: Analysts, GE upbeat on GE 1997 prospects.
newsitem.headline: Analysts, GE upbeat on GE 1997 prospects.

text.p: Analysts and General Electric Co agreed Thursday that the diversified giant was well-positioned for another year of record earnings in 1997.
GE earlier Thursday reported fourth quarter earnings per share of $1.26, up from $1.12 a year earlier. For the full year 1996, earnings were $4.40 a share, up from 1995's $3.90.
"The earnings are pretty much in line with expectations," said Steve O'Neil, an analyst at J.J.B. Hilliard, W.L. Lyons in Louisville.
At 1502 EST/2000 GMT, GE stock was down 1-1/2 to 101-1/8.
O'Neil said GE was expecting an even better 1997 based on likely improvments in its aircraft-engine, broadcasting and plastics businesses.
Growth would also be powered by an aggressive stock-buyback program and the acquisition-hungry GE Capital Services Inc, said O'Neil.
"This company more and more tries to determine its own fate instead of just letting the market sweep over it for better or worse," said Jeanne Terrile, analyst at Merrill Lynch.
"It is such a big company that it's tough to find the one ingredient that will add five percent to its growth rate," she said.
She said the company instead tries "to find a notion or concept, whether it's Six Sigma (quality control) or whatever, that (it) can apply to every piece of GE."
"This is exactly what GE has done for past two years," said Terrile. She said the company is on track to post 1997 earnings per share of $4.90-4.95 and 1998 earnings per share of $5.60-5.65.

Eleven of GE's 12 businesses reported higher operating profit for 1996, with five -- GE Capital Services, Power Systems, NBC, Medical Systems and Motors -- achieving double-digit increases in all activities.
In a statement, GE Chairman John Welch said earnings per share for the year increased 13 percent, and net income rose 11 percent to a record $7.28 billion.
Welch said the company is "confident that GE enters 1997 better-positioned than ever to deliver another year of record profits."
GE spokesman Bruce Bunch told Reuters the company's far-flung diversity in many different businesses would continue to pay off.
"As we look ahead, we know we'll always have some businesses with very strong performance," he said.
"We obviously have seen great growth and success in GE Capital and NBC, which are service businesses, and now we're applying the service mentality to our industrial businesses," said Bunch.
"They're now moving beyond repairing products to providing solutions for their customers."

Increasing globalization would play a bigger role in the company's growth, he said. International activities will make up about half of the company's revenues by the year 2000, compared with 40 percent in 1996 and 38 percent in 1995, said Bunch.

Bunch said that in 1997, GE will invest $300 million in its Six Sigma quality improvement program and expects $400-500 million in savings from the program, resulting in $100-200 million in operating margin improvements.
--Matthew Lewis, New York (212) 859-1902
